claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially exists in a high-temperature BCC state.
The range of phases formed in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by competition between diffusion-limited kinetic arrest and thermodynamic driving forces.
Rapid cooling can freeze in metastable phase configurations.
Slower cooling permits diffusion toward near-equilibrium phase distributions.
Extended isothermal holds permit diffusion toward near-equilibrium phase distributions.
Phase fractions and microstructural morphology in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 are sensitive to cooling rate.
Phase fractions, precipitate sizes, and precipitate distributions in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 are sensitive to isothermal hold time.
Rapid quenching reduces atomic mobility in the alloy.
Reduced atomic mobility during rapid quenching leads to heterogeneous nucleation of metastable phases.
Slower cooling enables sufficient diffusion for transformation toward equilibrium phase assemblages.
Rapidly quenched samples will contain a higher fraction of metastable phases than samples cooled at the moderate baseline rate.
Post-cooling isothermal holds will shift the alloy toward equilibrium microstructures by partially overcoming kinetic arrest.
A moderate cooling-rate baseline can yield a reproducible phase assemblage near equilibrium.
The proposed mechanism applies when the available diffusion time is comparable to the phase-transformation timescale.
The kinetic-arrest mechanism ceases to govern phase selection when cooling is sufficiently slow for equilibrium to be attained.
Impurity pinning or irradiation can overwhelm the proposed cooling-rate-controlled diffusion mechanism.
In Mn17Fe21Co24Ni24Cu14, varying cooling rate from the melt significantly changes the observed microstructure and phases.
In Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20, rapid versus slow cooling shifts the reported FCC crystallization temperature.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis proposes systematic variation of post-cooling hold duration and attributes equilibration to that variation, but the falsification design gives all samples identical isothermal holds. The rule nevertheless refers to variation in subsequent hold times, so the stated design cannot test the hold-duration component.
